description: Next.js provides automatic performance optimizations including Server Components (no client JS), code-splitting by route segment, prefetching via the <Link> component, image optimization via <Image>, font optimization via next/font, and script deferred loading via <Script>. Application-level performance requires intentional architecture: minimizing client bundle size, maximizing prerendering scope, eliminating data waterfalls, using streaming for slow content, and optimizing Core Web Vitals (LCP, CLS, INP). Performance is an architectural concern determined at design time, not a post-hoc optimization.

constraints.title: Minimize Client JavaScript Bundle — Push 'use client' to Leaf Nodes
constraints.problem: Client JavaScript bundle size directly determines Time to Interactive (TTI) and Interaction to Next Paint (INP). Placing 'use client' too high in the component tree unnecessarily includes server-renderable components in the client bundle.
constraints.whyItMatters: Every kilobyte in the client bundle must be downloaded, parsed, and executed before the page is fully interactive. Server Components contribute zero bytes to the client bundle. Maximizing the Server Component surface area is the most effective way to reduce TTI and improve Core Web Vitals. A single misplaced 'use client' on a parent component can pull in megabytes of server-only logic.
forbiddenPatterns: Adding 'use client' to layout.tsx or page.tsx when only a leaf component needs interactivity
Not using next/dynamic for large Client Components that are not needed immediately
Importing large third-party libraries into Client Components without tree-shaking verification
Using barrel imports (import * from 'large-library') in Client Components
Not using optimizePackageImports for icon libraries or large component suites
allowedPatterns: next/dynamic with lazy loading for non-critical Client Components
experimental.optimizePackageImports in next.config.js for large libraries
@next/bundle-analyzer to measure and monitor bundle composition
Explicit named imports instead of barrel imports
Server Components for all non-interactive UI
productionRisks: High TTI degrading user experience and INP Core Web Vital
Poor Lighthouse scores affecting SEO and reputation
Increased data transfer costs for users on metered connections
Slow page interactivity on low-end devices
architectureImplications: Bundle size is an architectural constraint, not a deployment concern
Every 'use client' boundary decision has a measurable bundle size impact
optimizationGuidance: Run @next/bundle-analyzer after every significant feature addition
Set a per-route JavaScript budget and enforce it in CI
Use next/dynamic with ssr: true for large Client Components that load below the fold
quickFixes: Move 'use client' from the parent layout to the specific interactive child component
Add next/dynamic lazy loading for a large Client Component
architectureSuggestions: Treat client JavaScript as a scarce resource: budget it per route, measure it continuously, and require justification for additions
Enable experimental.optimizePackageImports in next.config.js for all icon libraries and large component suites

constraints.title: Use next/image for All User-Facing Images
constraints.problem: Using raw HTML tags instead of Next.js's component bypasses automatic image optimization, modern format conversion (WebP/AVIF), responsive sizing, and Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) prevention.
constraints.whyItMatters: Images are typically the largest LCP element. Unoptimized images served in legacy formats (JPEG, PNG) with incorrect sizing contribute directly to poor LCP scores. Raw tags without explicit width/height cause CLS as images load and push content down. next/image automatically addresses all of these at zero additional code cost.
forbiddenPatterns: for user-visible images
Raw tags without explicit width and height (causes CLS)
Loading large images without lazy loading for below-the-fold content
Not using priority={true} on the LCP image (the largest above-the-fold image)
Not specifying sizes prop for responsive images, causing oversized image downloads on mobile
allowedPatterns: <Image src={...} width={800} height={600} alt='...' /> for fixed-size images
<Image src={...} fill alt='...' /> for images filling a container
<Image src={...} priority={true} /> for the LCP image
<Image src={...} loading='lazy' /> (default) for below-the-fold images
Specifying sizes prop for images that change size across breakpoints
productionRisks: Poor LCP scores from unoptimized large images
High bandwidth usage from uncompressed legacy formats
CLS from images loading without dimensions
SEO ranking impact from Core Web Vitals degradation
architectureImplications: Image optimization is an infrastructure concern; next/image handles it with zero configuration
The priority prop on the LCP image enables resource hint preloading — it is critical to set correctly
optimizationGuidance: Identify the LCP element on all key routes using Lighthouse or Chrome DevTools and add priority={true}
Configure next.config.js remotePatterns for all external image domains
quickFixes: Replace with from 'next/image'
architectureSuggestions: Create a shared Image component wrapper in components/ui/image.tsx that enforces alt text and default optimization settings

invalid: // No optimization, no size hints, potential CLS
valid:
import Image from 'next/image'
<Image src={product.imageUrl} width={400} height={400} alt={product.name} priority={isLCP} />

constraints.title: Use next/font to Eliminate Layout Shift from Web Fonts
constraints.problem: Loading web fonts via <link> tags to external CDNs (Google Fonts) causes network requests that delay font availability, produce Flash of Invisible Text (FOIT) or Flash of Unstyled Text (FOUT), and contribute to Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS).
constraints.whyItMatters: CLS from font loading is one of the most common Core Web Vitals failures. next/font automatically self-hosts fonts alongside the application's static assets, applies size-adjust to eliminate layout shift, and generates CSS variables for convenient usage. It removes the external network request entirely and is zero-runtime-cost.
forbiddenPatterns: <link href='https://fonts.googleapis.com/...' rel='stylesheet'> in layout.tsx
Importing fonts from CDNs in _document.tsx or global CSS @import
Using @font-face with remote URLs without size-adjust declarations
Loading multiple font weights and styles unnecessarily (inflates CSS and font files)
allowedPatterns: import { Inter } from 'next/font/google'; const inter = Inter({ subsets: ['latin'] })
import localFont from 'next/font/local'; for self-hosted fonts
Applying the font className to the root <html> element
Using CSS variables (variable: '--font-inter') for flexible usage in Tailwind
productionRisks: CLS degradation from font-swap layout shifts
External network dependency on Google Fonts CDN (single point of failure, latency, privacy)
FOUT (Flash of Unstyled Text) degrading perceived quality
architectureImplications: Font loading strategy is a layout-level concern; apply the font class to the root HTML element in layout.tsx
optimizationGuidance: Load only the font weights and styles actually used in the design
Use the display: 'swap' option (default) or display: 'optional' for performance-critical text
quickFixes: Replace the <link> Google Fonts import with next/font/google
Apply the font className to the <html> element in root layout

constraints.title: Use next/script to Load Third-Party Scripts Without Blocking Rendering
constraints.problem: Including third-party scripts (analytics, chat widgets, ad pixels) via raw <script> tags in the document head blocks HTML parsing and delays First Contentful Paint (FCP) and Largest Contentful Paint (LCP).
constraints.whyItMatters: Render-blocking scripts are one of the most impactful causes of poor Web Vitals. Every millisecond spent downloading and executing a third-party script delays the first pixel painted to the user's screen. next/script provides declarative loading strategies (afterInteractive, lazyOnload, worker) that defer non-critical scripts until after the page is interactive.
forbiddenPatterns: <script src='https://analytics.example.com/script.js'> in the <head> without defer or async
<script> tags in layout.tsx without next/script
Loading analytics or tracking pixels synchronously in the head
The worker strategy for scripts in the App Router (not supported; use afterInteractive or lazyOnload)
allowedPatterns: <Script src={url} strategy='afterInteractive' /> for analytics that need to load after page becomes interactive
<Script src={url} strategy='lazyOnload' /> for chat widgets and non-critical scripts
<Script src={url} strategy='beforeInteractive' /> only for scripts that must run before hydration (rare)
Using the onLoad callback for scripts that require post-load initialization
productionRisks: Render-blocking scripts significantly degrading FCP and LCP
Poor Core Web Vitals scores from slow third-party scripts
Main thread blocking from synchronous script execution during parse
architectureImplications: Third-party script loading strategy is an architectural decision; choose the most deferred strategy that meets the script's requirements
afterInteractive is the safe default for most analytics and tracking scripts
optimizationGuidance: Audit all third-party scripts and assign the most deferred strategy possible
Monitor third-party script impact on Web Vitals using Lighthouse and Chrome User Experience Report (CrUX)
quickFixes: Replace <script src='...'> with <Script src='...' strategy='afterInteractive' /> from 'next/script'
architectureSuggestions: Evaluate whether every third-party script is actually required; each one adds risk to Web Vitals. Remove unused scripts.

constraints.title: Lazy Load Non-Critical Client Components with next/dynamic
constraints.problem: All Client Components referenced in a route's module graph are bundled together and loaded upfront, even if some components are only visible after user interaction (modals, drawers, tooltips, advanced settings panels).
constraints.whyItMatters: Components that are not visible on initial load (modals, accordions, tabs not in the default tab) can defer their JavaScript download until needed. next/dynamic enables code-splitting at the component level, reducing the initial JavaScript payload and improving TTI.
forbiddenPatterns: Statically importing large modal or drawer components that are conditionally shown
Statically importing rich text editors, code editors, or complex chart libraries for features behind interactions
Not using next/dynamic for components heavier than 50KB that are not immediately visible
allowedPatterns: const Modal = dynamic(() => import('./modal'), { loading: () => <Skeleton />, ssr: true }) for heavy conditionally-shown components
Lazy loading rich text editors, code editors, PDF viewers, map components
Using the loading prop to provide a meaningful placeholder during dynamic import resolution
productionRisks: Inflated initial JavaScript bundle from eagerly loading non-critical components
Poor TTI from unnecessary JavaScript parsing and execution
Wasted bandwidth for users who never trigger the condition to show the lazy-loaded component
architectureImplications: Code splitting is an explicit architectural decision in Next.js; it requires using next/dynamic to opt in at the component level
Server Components provide route-level code splitting automatically; Client Components require explicit dynamic() for component-level splitting
optimizationGuidance: Identify the top 5 heaviest Client Components via @next/bundle-analyzer and evaluate lazy loading each
Default to dynamic() for any Client Component that contains a library import heavier than 30KB
quickFixes: Wrap the import: const HeavyComponent = dynamic(() => import('./heavy'), { loading: () => <Skeleton /> })
architectureSuggestions: Establish a rule: any Client Component with a unique library dependency exceeding 30KB gzipped must use dynamic() unless it is above-the-fold and critical path

invalid: import RichTextEditor from './rich-text-editor' // 200KB library, loaded for all users even if they never edit
valid:
import dynamic from 'next/dynamic'
const RichTextEditor = dynamic(() => import('./rich-text-editor'), { loading: () => <Skeleton className='h-64' />, ssr: false })

constraints.title: Request-time APIs in Root Layout Degrade the Entire Application's Performance
constraints.problem: Using cookies(), headers(), or searchParams in the root layout.tsx without Suspense wrapping forces the entire application into dynamic rendering, eliminating all prerendering benefits for every route.
constraints.whyItMatters: The root layout wraps every route in the application. Any dynamic rendering opt-in at the root layout level propagates to all child routes. A single cookies() call in app/layout.tsx without Suspense means zero static HTML is served for any route — every page view requires server compute.
forbiddenPatterns: cookies() in app/layout.tsx at the top level without Suspense
headers() in app/layout.tsx at the top level without Suspense
useSearchParams() in a component imported by app/layout.tsx without Suspense
Any runtime data access at the root layout level without Suspense isolation
allowedPatterns: Wrapping runtime API consumers in Suspense in the root layout
Using Partial Prerendering (PPR) to keep the static shell while streaming dynamic sections
Reading cookies in a deep child component wrapped in Suspense rather than the layout
productionRisks: Entire application becomes dynamically rendered, destroying CDN cacheability
Every page view incurs server compute cost regardless of content type
TTFB degrades from CDN-level to server-compute-level for every route
architectureImplications: Root layout should be static or nearly static
Per-user customization belongs in child route segments wrapped in Suspense, not the root layout
optimizationGuidance: Audit app/layout.tsx for any runtime API usage and extract it into a child component wrapped in Suspense
quickFixes: Extract the cookies() call into a child component: <Suspense fallback={<StaticUI />}><DynamicContent /></Suspense>
architectureSuggestions: Design the root layout as a static skeleton (HTML structure, fonts, global providers) with dynamic user-specific content loaded lazily in child segments

valid:
// app/layout.tsx — static shell
export default function RootLayout({ children }) { return <html lang='en'><body><Suspense fallback={null}><LocaleProvider /></Suspense>{children}</body></html> }
